data.title: How Investors May Respond To Lennar (LEN) Misleading Disclosure Lawsuit
data.description:
• Lennar is facing a class action lawsuit filed in November 2026 that claims the company misled investors about its operating approach and the true purpose of the Millrose spin off, including how expenses were recorded and how affiliated transactions affected reported demand.
  • The complaint highlights an alleged use of Millrose to buy Lennar homes at above market prices and rent them at below market levels. If accurate, these practices would raise fundamental questions about how the homebuilder’s asset light model and demand trends were presented to shareholders.
  • This article examines how Lennar's investment narrative is challenged by alleged Millrose related home purchases used to support reported demand.
Spot fresh housing plays by comparing Lennar's legal and demand risks against a curated list of solid balance sheet and fundamentals (25 results) that are not relying on complex structures to support reported performance.

Lennar Investment Narrative Recap

To own Lennar, an investor needs to be comfortable with a homebuilder that relies heavily on an asset light model, tight build cycles and controlled homesites rather than a large land bank. The class action and Millrose allegations cut across that story because they question how land option costs and affiliated transactions intersect with the reported asset mix and demand.

In the short term, the key swing factor remains housing demand under high mortgage rates and Lennar’s ability to keep volumes moving with incentives while protecting already compressed 4.1% profit margins. The biggest risk now is that legal and regulatory scrutiny around Millrose raises compliance costs or constrains use of similar structures at a time when affordability pressure is already weighing on deliveries.

The lawsuit itself is the central development to focus on. Robbins LLP alleges Lennar capitalized expenses tied to land bank option agreements, rather than expensing them, and used Millrose to purchase homes above market prices while renting them below market levels. That critique goes directly to the analyst consensus narrative on Simply Wall St, which was built around the benefits of an asset and land light approach.

If the court process leads to tighter limits on affiliated land bank activity, the homebuilder may have less flexibility in how it balances reported margins, demand optics and land access. For you, the operational questions are whether Lennar can still sustain its volume focused production model, keep construction costs around US$80 per square foot under control and manage higher land and option fees without further pressure on earnings.

Lennar's analyst narrative points to revenues of US$40.6b and earnings of US$2.7b by 2029, based on assumed annual revenue growth of 8.3% and an earnings increase of about US$1.4b from US$1.3b today.

Their bigger worry is demand, not accounting, so this lawsuit could push those already cautious forecasts even lower or be reassessed entirely.

data.title: What Nickel Industries Bears Saw Before The Fall
data.description:
If you had skipped Nickel Industries at the start of 2026, it might feel like you simply sidestepped another noisy battery-metal story. Investors who held Nickel Industries from the start of the year are down 36.1%, including dividends. That outcome turned a bullish December 2025 narrative about Hengjaya, ENC HPAL and EV exposure into a painful hold. The real question is which funding, regulatory, or demand assumptions were already on record that could have challenged that optimism.

If the move has made Nickel Industries harder to judge, start where the gap is still open and scan 2 high quality undervalued stocks.

The Two Stories Investors Had To Weigh On Nickel Industries

The shares cost A$0.83 at the start of the period, and anyone looking at Nickel Industries then had to choose between two sharply different stories about where the business could head next.

On the upbeat side, the Hengjaya and ENC HPAL narrative pointed to a Fair Value of A$0.97. This price was implied by expectations of expanded production, more nickel sulphate and cathode exposure, and improved ESG credentials supporting customer demand.

The bearish July 2025 view argued for a Fair Value of A$0.65. This was based on the risk that nickel demand could shrink as LFP batteries gained ground and tighter ESG rules pushed Indonesian operating costs higher.

What The Results Changed For Nickel Industries

The clearest new fact was Nickel Industries lifting H1 revenue to US$938.4m and net income to US$52.5m, with net margin moving from 1.4% to 5.6%. That improved profitability pointed toward a more positive view of the Hengjaya and ENC HPAL operations. Funding concerns around the US$245m ENC facility and higher project debt pulled in the opposite direction, so the period had both positive and negative elements rather than resolving the debate.

The lesson for readers is straightforward. When a growth narrative relies on large-scale projects, it is useful to track net margin and funding mix side by side, and to reassess them with every result and financing announcement.

What You Are Being Asked To Believe About Nickel Industries Today

Nickel Industries now trades at A$0.57, after a 36.1% loss from the start of the year. The analyst consensus Narrative on Simply Wall St views its Fair Value as sitting above that price, based on a shift toward higher margin battery-grade products and tighter Indonesian ore supply.

That Narrative argues the drop only looks attractive if you think ENC funding demands, water constraints and ore availability can be handled well enough for higher value output to come through. data.title: Companies Like Sky Metals (ASX:SKY) Are In A Position To Invest In Growth
data.description:
We can readily understand why investors are attracted to unprofitable companies. For example, although software-as-a-service business Salesforce.com lost money for years while it grew recurring revenue, if you held shares since 2005, you'd have done very well indeed. Nonetheless, only a fool would ignore the risk that a loss making company burns through its cash too quickly.

So, the natural question for Sky Metals (ASX:SKY) shareholders is whether they should be concerned by its rate of cash burn. In this article, we define cash burn as its annual (negative) free cash flow, which is the amount of money a company spends each year to fund its growth. The first step is to compare its cash burn with its cash reserves, to give us its 'cash runway'.

AI is about to change healthcare. These 20 stocks are working on everything from early diagnostics to drug discovery. The best part - they are all under $10bn in marketcap - there is still time to get in early.

Does Sky Metals Have A Long Cash Runway?

You can calculate a company's cash runway by dividing the amount of cash it has by the rate at which it is spending that cash. As at June 2026, Sky Metals had cash of AU$18m and no debt. Looking at the last year, the company burnt through AU$11m. So it had a cash runway of approximately 20 months from June 2026. Notably, analysts forecast that Sky Metals will break even (at a free cash flow level) in about 3 years. That means unless the company reduces its cash burn quickly, it may well look to raise more cash. Depicted below, you can see how its cash holdings have changed over time.

See our latest analysis for Sky Metals

How Is Sky Metals' Cash Burn Changing Over Time?

Sky Metals didn't record any revenue over the last year, indicating that it's an early stage company still developing its business. So while we can't look to sales to understand growth, we can look at how the cash burn is changing to understand how expenditure is trending over time. In fact, it ramped its spending strongly over the last year, increasing cash burn by 102%. That sort of spending growth rate can't continue for very long before it causes balance sheet weakness, generally speaking. Clearly, however, the crucial factor is whether the company will grow its business going forward. So you might want to take a peek at how much the company is expected to grow in the next few years.

How Hard Would It Be For Sky Metals To Raise More Cash For Growth?

While Sky Metals does have a solid cash runway, its cash burn trajectory may have some shareholders thinking ahead to when the company may need to raise more cash. Generally speaking, a listed business can raise new cash through issuing shares or taking on debt. Commonly, a business will sell new shares in itself to raise cash and drive growth. By comparing a company's annual cash burn to its total market capitalisation, we can estimate roughly how many shares it would have to issue in order to run the company for another year (at the same burn rate).

Since it has a market capitalisation of AU$119m, Sky Metals' AU$11m in cash burn equates to about 9.1% of its market value. That's a low proportion, so we figure the company would be able to raise more cash to fund growth, with a little dilution, or even to simply borrow some money.

So, Should We Worry About Sky Metals' Cash Burn?

Even though its increasing cash burn makes us a little nervous, we are compelled to mention that we thought Sky Metals' cash burn relative to its market cap was relatively promising. One real positive is that analysts are forecasting that the company will reach breakeven. Cash burning companies are always on the riskier side of things, but after considering all of the factors discussed in this short piece, we're not too worried about its rate of cash burn.
